items.name: RESTer
items.source_story_title: Postman silently auto-installs AI plugins and attempts to share all API data
items.summary: Firefox API-testing extension; a user prefers its lightweight, browser-native approach.
items.why_included: A direct first-hand alternative to installing a desktop API client.
items.evidence: A RESTer user describes testing APIs in Firefox and prefers the lighter browser-based workflow.

evidence_sources.author: wackget
evidence_sources.excerpt: I much prefer the approach of being able to use the browser for things like this. It feels much more lightweight than installing a piece of desktop software.

items.name: Yaak
items.source_story_title: Postman silently auto-installs AI plugins and attempts to share all API data
items.summary: API client recommended for restoring a simple workflow after Insomnia's account push.
items.why_included: An explicit recommendation grounded in a user's switch from Insomnia.
items.evidence: An Insomnia user switched to Yaak for a simpler API-client experience and strongly recommends it.

evidence_sources.author: amflare

items.name: rustic
items.source_story_title: Fujifilm to boost tape production 5x as AI fuels archiving demand
items.summary: Backup tool with Glacier Deep Archive support; recommended for secondary, rarely restored backups.
items.why_included: A year-long user and contributor offers a concrete alternative to buying tape hardware.
items.evidence: A rustic user and contributor recommends Glacier Deep Archive cold storage, explicitly advising secondary-backup use rather than routine restores.

evidence_sources.author: pmw
evidence_sources.excerpt: I heartily recommend rustic's cold storage support for Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive. It ends up being $1/TB/month, as long as you plan to not restore from it. (Use it as a secondary backup, and plan to restore from your primary.) I have been using rustic+GDA for about a year now, and I contributed some enhancements to this software ecosystem to make this path smooth for others.

items.name: Toit
items.summary: ESP32 programming language; a repeat user praises its clean syntax and working tools.
items.why_included: Concrete project experience supports the praise, with a disclosed family connection to a developer.
items.evidence: A user praises Toit's language and tooling across projects and reports no performance problems, while disclosing that floitsch is their brother.

evidence_sources.author: close2
evidence_sources.excerpt: I have used toit in a lot of my projects. It is a really nice language and so much cleaner than all the alternatives I have tried (Arduino, Python, Lua). The tools just work and I got used to the language really quickly. I did hate that it was bytecode. It just felt wrong to run bytecode on an ESP32. OTOH it just works, and I have never noticed any performance problems. My latest project is a controller for a slave-clock: https://gitlab.com/close2/nebenuhr-toit (There is also a Garmin repository that allows me to control the clock using my Garmin watch.) Full disclosure: I had to use toit (floitsch is my brother), but it really is a nice language and development environment.

items.name: Flipper Zero
items.source_story_title: Preparing for the Flipper One Kickstarter and opening pre-orders
items.summary: Portable electronics multitool; an owner praises hands-on signal experiments and NFC learning with kids.
items.why_included: The existing Flipper Zero receives concrete ownership praise, distinct from preorder enthusiasm for Flipper One.
items.evidence: A Flipper Zero owner describes frequent signal experiments and enjoyable NFC-based educational activities with children.

evidence_sources.author: vr46
evidence_sources.excerpt: My F0 is always close at hand, doing everything from being my go-to trigger for whatever random thing I'm playing with, to being an instant output for any signal I'm trying to read. Plus it's a really fun educational tool for myself and various kids around - I keep a load of little NFC 216 tags around, in my bag, in a pouch attached to my Mac, and showing both young and old how to use them, and read them with the phone, leads to conversations about treasure hunts, hiding them in the pub, showing counters with amusing messages...
